crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

children.name: The AI Enablement Audit
children.blurb: The AI Enablement Audit is a structured review of whether an organization can adopt AI tools and workflows without creating unmanaged security, privacy, or legal exposure.

children.name: Threat Modelling for Legal AI
children.blurb: Threat modelling for legal AI is the structured practice of identifying, prioritising, and mitigating threats to AI systems used in legal work, including legal research, drafting, contract review, e-discovery, and matter management.

children.name: Data Loss Prevention and Sanitisation
children.blurb: Data loss prevention and sanitisation in AI covers the controls that keep sensitive data from leaving an organisation through prompts, outputs, training pipelines, retrieval stores, logs, and agent actions.

children.name: Shadow AI in Legal Teams
children.blurb: Shadow AI in legal teams covers any use of artificial intelligence tools by lawyers, paralegals, legal operations staff, or outside counsel without review or approval from the firm's or department's security, privacy, and legal operations functions.

children.name: Bias Testing and Alignment
children.blurb: Bias testing and alignment covers the measurement of how a model's outputs differ across groups and the work of steering those outputs toward stated goals and policies.

sections.body: AI security audits and enterprise enablement is the work of letting a law firm or legal department use artificial intelligence without losing control of its data, its duties or its judgement. In practice this means auditing which tools staff already reach for, modelling how a legal model could be attacked or misled, scrubbing sensitive material before it leaves the building, finding the tools nobody approved, and testing whether a model treats people and matters even handedly. The site tracks 850 AI tools, and a legal team cannot audit what it has not inventoried, so much of this work begins as a counting exercise. It is closer to facilities management than to research, because the job is keeping a live system safe rather than proving a theorem.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The inventory and policy side is largely solved in outline. Firms can list approved tools, classify data, and write rules about what may be pasted into a chat window. Detection of shadow AI is harder, because staff adopt new tools faster than any register is updated, and blocking everything simply pushes the use underground. Threat modelling for legal models is still young, since the attack surface changes with every model update and few legal teams have the security staff to keep pace. Bias testing is the least settled area, because there is no agreed standard for what a fair legal model looks like, and a test that passes on one matter may say nothing about the next. The honest limit across all of it is that audits produce evidence of effort, not proof of safety.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The AI Enablement Audit is the entry point, setting out how a firm takes stock of its tools, data flows and gaps before anything else is attempted. Threat Modelling for Legal AI then asks what could go wrong with the models a firm has chosen to keep, from prompt injection to leakage through outputs. Data Loss Prevention and Sanitisation deals with the material itself, covering how confidential content is stripped, masked or kept out of external systems. Shadow AI in Legal Teams addresses the tools that never entered the register, which is where most real incidents begin. Bias Testing and Alignment closes the set by examining whether a model's outputs hold up across different clients, matters and fact patterns. Read together they form a cycle of inventory, threat, control, discovery and testing rather than a one time checklist.
